L0@P0: WAVE: A Decentralized Authorization Framework with Transitive Delegation
L1@P0: Michael P Andersen, Sam Kumar, Moustafa AbdelBaky
L2@P0: Gabe Fierro, John Kolb, Hyung-Sin Kim, David E. Culler, Raluca Ada Popa
L3@P0: University of California, Berkeley
L4@P0: Abstract
L5@P0: Most deployed authorization systems rely on a central
L6@P0: trusted service whose compromise can lead to the breach
L7@P0: of millions of user accounts and permissions. We present
L8@P0: WAVE, an authorization framework offering decentralized
L9@P0: trust: no central services can modify or see permissions and
L10@P0: any participant can delegate a portion of their permissions
L11@P0: autonomously. To achieve this goal, WAVE adopts an expressive authorization model, enforces it cryptographically,
L12@P0: protects permissions via a novel encryption protocol while
L13@P0: enabling discovery of permissions, and stores them in an untrusted scalable storage solution. WAVE provides competitive performance to traditional authorization systems relying
L14@P0: on central trust. It is an open-source artifact and has been
L15@P0: used for two years for controlling 800 IoT devices.
L16@P0: 1 Introduction
L17@P0: Authorization and authentication are fundamental components of many systems. Most authorization systems today
L18@P0: rely on centralized services such as centralized credential
L19@P0: stores (e.g., [15, 19, 56]), Access Control Lists (ACLs), Active Directory, and OAuth [4]. For example, in a calendar
L20@P0: application, a central service stores which users have access
L21@P0: to what calendars, and users authenticate to it, e.g. via username and password. In these systems, delegation is critical:
L22@P0: for instance, allowing an assistant to edit your calendar, and
L23@P0: letting the assistant further delegate restrictive view access to
L24@P0: an event organizer. These forms of delegation are typically
L25@P0: implemented as changes to a centralized ACL.
L26@P0: However, this approach presents two fundamental problems. First, a centralized service is a central point of attack:
L27@P0: a single attack can simultaneously compromise many user
L28@P0: accounts and permissions. There have been numerous such
L29@P0: breaches [39], and attackers even managed to log in as the
L30@P0: victim users. Second, the operator of the central server has
L31@P0: a complete view of the private permission data for all users
L32@P0: (thus seeing users’ social relationships [54]), and can modify
L33@P0: permissions [2].
L34@P0: Responding to the weaknesses of centralized systems, recent security systems are increasingly avoiding a trusted
L35@P0: central service. This approach has been adopted by endto-end encryption systems [25], such as WhatsApp and
L36@P0: Signal, blockchains (e.g., Bitcoin, Ethereum, Zcash), or
L37@P0: ledgers (e.g., IBM’s Hyperledger [17], Certificate Transparency [41], Key Transparency [32]). Our goal is to build a
L38@P0: scalable decentralized authorization system, permitting delegation under a similar threat model.
L39@P0: We propose a decentralized authorization system that
L40@P0: does not rely on a trusted service, WAVE (“WAVE is an
L41@P0: Authorization Verification Engine”). WAVE offers decentralized trust: each user’s WAVE client manages the
L42@P0: permissions of that user and can delegate access to other
L43@P0: users. WAVE enforces delegation cryptographically, not via
L44@P0: a trusted service. It aims to capture a wide range of authorization policies and to provide an alternative to traditional
L45@P0: systems, such as OAuth [4] and Active Directory.
L46@P0: Importantly, in providing decentralized transitive delegation, WAVE facilitates applications that span multiple trust
L47@P0: domains. For example, IoT orchestration applications like
L48@P0: If This Then That (IFTTT) [3] tie together multiple vendors and users, but IFTTT’s design relies on several central
L49@P0: points of attack: the vendor OAuth servers and the IFTTT
L50@P0: token storage servers. The compromise of any one of these
L51@P0: servers may affect hundreds of thousands of users. Using WAVE, greater cross-administrative-domain orchestration can be achieved with no central authorization servers,
L52@P0: reducing the trust that each domain must place in the others.
L53@P0: 1.1 Usage Scenarios
L54@P0: While authorization plays a key role in the security of almost any system today, the benefits of decentralized authorization are most pronounced in systems that are inherently distributed, where the prevailing centralized authorization schemes undermine what would otherwise be a resilient
L55@P0: system. Our deployment of WAVE over the past two years
L56@P0: has focused on securing distributed IoT devices and services
L57@P0: used to monitor and control over twenty small to mediumsized commercial and residential buildings; hence, we will
L58@P0: use smart buildings as a running example.
L59@P0: Consider a set of campuses, each owned by a property
L60@P0: manager. Each campus is composed of multiple buildings,
L61@P0: with portions of each building leased out to tenants by the
L62@P0: property manager. The property manager within each campus is the authority for the cyberphysical resources associated with the buildings in the campus, but they must delegate
L63@P0: permission to the individual building managers who must
L64@P0: further delegate permissions to the tenants, allowing them
L65@P0: to control the portions of the buildings that they rent. Any of
L66@P0: these principals may then further delegate permissions to IoT
L67@P0: devices, long-running analytics or control services operating
L68@P0: on their behalf, perhaps provided by the utility. The building
L69@P0: manager and/or tenant will also grant ephemeral permissions
L70@P0: on subsets of the building infrastructure to contractors (like
L71@P0: HVAC commissioning teams) and, especially in our case, to
L72@P0-1: 1researchers.
L73@P1: A similar structure occurs in small residential buildings
L74@P1: where a homeowner installs smart devices such as lights and
L75@P1: thermostats and needs to delegate permission on those devices to their partner, guest, nanny, or children.
L76@P1: Cross-administrative-domain delegation is present in both
L77@P1: examples. In larger buildings, we see the boundary between
L78@P1: the property owner and the tenants. In residential buildings, this is most evident when using orchestration tools like
L79@P1: IFTTT, where an organization, distinct from the owner of the
L80@P1: devices, runs the controller service and needs to obtain permission from the owner.
L81@P1: WAVE is not limited to IoT. It provides general purpose
L82@P1: delegable authorization and can, for example, be used in
L83@P1: place of OAuth to remove the risk of the centralized tokenissuing server and allow for richer delegation semantics.
L84@P1: 1.2 High-Level Security Goal & Threat Model
L85@P1: At a high level, our objective is to design a system where the
L86@P1: compromise of an authorization server does not compromise
L87@P1: all the users’ permissions. Namely, even if an adversary has
L88@P1: compromised any authorization servers and users, it should
L89@P1: not be able to:
L90@P1: 1. Grant permissions on behalf of uncompromised users.

L0@P0: Horcrux: A Password Manager for Paranoids
L1@P0: Hannah Li, David Evans
L2@P0: University of Virginia
L3@P0: [hannahli,evans]@virginia.edu
L4@P0: ABSTRACT
L5@P0: Vulnerabilities in password managers are unremitting because current designs provide large attack surfaces, both at the client and
L6@P0: server. We describe and evaluate Horcrux, a password manager
L7@P0: that is designed holistically to minimize and decentralize trust,
L8@P0: while retaining the usability of a traditional password manager.
L9@P0: The prototype Horcrux client, implemented as a Firefox add-on, is
L10@P0: split into two components, with code that has access to the user’s
L11@P0: master’s password and any key material isolated into a small auditable component, separate from the complexity of managing the
L12@P0: user interface. Instead of exposing actual credentials to the DOM,
L13@P0: a dummy username and password are autofilled by the untrusted
L14@P0: component. The trusted component intercepts and modifies POST
L15@P0: requests before they are encrypted and sent over the network. To
L16@P0: avoid trusting a centralized store, stored credentials are secretshared over multiple servers. To provide domain and username
L17@P0: privacy, while maintaining resilience to off-line attacks on a compromised password store, we incorporate cuckoo hashing in a way
L18@P0: that ensures an attacker cannot determine if a guessed master password is correct. Our approach only works for websites that do not

L21@P0: KEYWORDS
L22@P0: password managers, privacy, secure system design, secret sharing
L23@P0: 1 INTRODUCTION
L24@P0: Users are frequently beseeched to come up with unique, strong
L25@P0: passwords for every on-line account, but remembering more than
L26@P0: a few high-entropy passwords is well beyond the capabilities of
L27@P0: normal humans. Das reported that 43–51% of Internet users reuse
L28@P0: the same password across multiple sites [12]. According to a recent survey of security experts, using a password manager was
L29@P0: among the most widely-accepted recommendations for improving
L30@P0: security [24].
L31@P0: Current password managers, however, do not provide adequate
L32@P0: protection for paranoid users. Vulnerabilities are frequently discovered in both the client and server components, as revealed in
L33@P0: several recent reports of compromises to major commercial password managers [23, 27, 47, 48]. Password managers which store user
L34@P0: credentials in cloud databases have been susceptible to theft and
L35@P0: successful dictionary attacks on stolen encrypted data, according to
L36@P0: recent news reports on LastPass [49] and KeePass [23]. Password
L37@P0: manager critics often cite database theft as a compelling reason not
L38@P0: to use password managers: “when password managers fail, they
L39@P0: offer a one-stop destination for hackers to obtain all of a target’s
L40@P0: passwords” [23].
L41@P0: Contributions. We present the comprehensive design and evaluation of a password manager, Horcrux,1
L42@P0: , that provides a level
L43@P0: of security and privacy well beyond what is achieved by current
L44@P0: systems. Horcrux is designed to minimize exposure of secrets to a
L45@P0: small, auditable component. Although our design is intended for
L46@P0: direct integration into a browser (see Section 7), we have demonstrated and evaluated its effectiveness by implementing a prototype
L47@P0: as an open source Firefox add-on (Section 5).
L48@P0: Our server side design (Section 3.2) distributes trust by using
L49@P0: secret sharing to store passwords across multiple hosts, and makes
L50@P0: novel use of cuckoo hashing to provide user and domain privacy
L51@P0: without enabling off-line attacks on password stores. Our client
L52@P0: design isolates the component that has access to passwords from
L53@P0: the rest of the password manager. Horcrux never exposes the credentials to the DOM, minimizing exposure of user credentials by
L54@P0: replacing autofilled dummy credentials with real credentials in outgoing network traffic (Section 3.3). Ideas similar to the password
L55@P0: swapping in intercepted outgoing network traffic we use have been
L56@P0: proposed before [46], but not adopted by password managers due
L57@P0: to usability and compatibility concerns. To evaluate the deployability of our design, we conducted a large-scale study of Alexa’s top
L58@P0: million websites. As reported in Section 6, we find that Horcrux
L59@P0: appears to be compatible with 98% of the websites where a login
L60@P0: form was found.
L61@P0: Security researchers have long advocated for minimizing trusted
L62@P0: computing bases [13, 30, 42] and using privilege separation [8,
L63@P0: 41], and secret-sharing is a well established technique [43]. The
L64@P0: main contribution of this work is combining established techniques
L65@P0: and our privacy-preserving credential storing scheme in a holistic
L66@P0: way to solve an important security problem, and performing a
L67@P0: comprehensive evaluation of both the security and compatibility
L68@P0: of that design.
